shared_context.topic: difference between canker sore and herpes

atoms.1: The distinction between a canker sore and herpes can be challenging.
atoms.2: There are clinical features that can help differentiate between a canker sore and herpes.
atoms.3: Canker sores are more common than herpes infections.
atoms.4: Canker sores usually present as a single lesion within the oral cavity.
atoms.5: Herpes infections often present with multiple lesions.
atoms.6: Canker sores typically heal within 7-14 days.
atoms.7: Canker sores are limited to the oral mucosa.
atoms.8: Herpes infections can persist for longer than canker sores.
atoms.9: Herpes infections are associated with viral shedding.
atoms.10: Patients with canker sores often report a history of recurring lesions.
atoms.11: Patients with herpes infections may report a history of multiple episodes of oral herpes.
atoms.12: Patients with herpes infections may report a history of multiple episodes of genital herpes.
atoms.13: Prodromal symptoms are often reported by patients with herpes infections.
atoms.14: Prodromal symptoms are not typically reported by patients with canker sores.
atoms.15: Canker sores are typically smaller and more shallow than herpes lesions.
atoms.16: Canker sores have a well-defined border.
atoms.17: Herpes lesions can be larger and more diffuse than canker sores.
atoms.18: Herpes lesions have a less distinct border than canker sores.
atoms.19: These clinical features are not always reliable.
atoms.20: A definitive diagnosis often requires laboratory confirmation.
atoms.21: Laboratory tests can help differentiate between canker sores and herpes.
atoms.22: A viral culture can confirm the presence of herpes simplex virus.
atoms.23: PCR can confirm the presence of herpes simplex virus.
atoms.24: Some patients may experience overlapping symptoms between canker sores and herpes.
atoms.25: Overlapping symptoms can make it challenging to make a definitive diagnosis without further testing.

snippets.output: The distinction between a canker sore and herpes can be challenging, but there are clinical features that can help differentiate between the two.
Prodromal symptoms are often reported by patients with herpes infections but not typically with canker sores.
Canker sores are typically smaller and more shallow, with a well-defined border, whereas herpes lesions can be larger and more diffuse, with a less distinct border.
These clinical features are not always reliable, and a definitive diagnosis often requires laboratory confirmation.
Laboratory tests can help differentiate between the two; for example, a viral culture or PCR can confirm the presence of herpes simplex virus.
Some patients may experience overlapping symptoms between canker sores and herpes, making it challenging to make a definitive diagnosis without further testing.
Canker sores typically heal within 7–14 days, whereas herpes infections can persist longer than canker sores.
Canker sores are limited to the oral mucosa.
Herpes infections are associated with viral shedding.
Canker sores are more common than herpes infections.
Canker sores usually present as a single lesion within the oral cavity, whereas herpes infections often present with multiple lesions.
snippets.notes: #4–#5 are on the same comparison axis, namely lesion number/presentation, whereas #3 is about prevalence, so it introduces a different dimension.

snippets.output: People with canker sores often report a history of recurring lesions, while people with herpes infections may report a history of multiple episodes of oral herpes.
snippets.notes: #10–#11 form a coherent snippet because both concern recurrence history relevant to distinguishing recurrent canker sores from recurrent oral herpes

snippets.output: Patients with herpes infections may report a history of multiple episodes of genital herpes.
snippets.notes: #12 is less directly aligned with the oral comparison, since a history of genital herpes is only indirectly informative, so it is better kept separate.
